slides.title: Dictionaries and Structuring Data
slides.say: Welcome to chapter 7. A dictionary stores pairs of a key and a value, and you ask by key. In this chapter we count with it, model a chessboard, copy it and write it down as text. Every result is really run. Ask the class: where have you used a phone book?

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Here is the route. Five parts take us from one pair to a chessboard, and each range is a run of slides you can jump to. Every code slide matches one example on the chapter page. Ask the class: which part do you expect to be hardest, and why?

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: These five questions are the chapter. Keep them in mind: each part of the deck answers some of them, and the summary answers all five in a line each. Example: question two asks which values may be keys. Ask the class to guess the answer before we reach part one.

slides.title: Part 1: The dictionary and its keys
slides.say: Part one introduces the dictionary data type. A dictionary holds key-value pairs, a key must be hashable, and since Python 3.7 the keys remember the order in which they were added. Ask the class: why can a tuple be a key?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the dictionary and its keys
slides.say: A dictionary is a phone book: look up the name and the number sits beside it. The key is the ticket at a coat check and the value is the coat. Example: a locker numbered by hair colour is lost when the hair changes. Ask the class: why must a key never change?

slides.title: Dictionary: pairs found by key
slides.say: A dictionary stores pairs of a key and a value, and you ask by key. Example: my_cat holds size, color and age. Python looks the key up directly, however many pairs there are. Ask the class: what would you use as keys for your own phone contacts?

slides.title: A dictionary holds key-value pairs
slides.say: Run the code and read the three lines it prints. The key size finds fat, the color is joined into a sentence, and len counts the pairs, not the characters. Ask the class to predict each line before the run, then check the table.

slides.title: Dictionaries and lists name things differently
slides.say: A list names items by position and a dictionary by key. Example: two lists with the same items in another order are not equal, but two dictionaries with the same pairs are equal. Ask the class: when does the order of items carry the meaning, and when only the names?

slides.title: Dictionaries versus lists
slides.say: Compare the first two lines: False for the lists and True for the dictionaries. The last line shows that the dictionary still remembers the order of adding. Example: the keys of ham print as name, age and species in the order they were typed. Ask the class: why can both statements be true at once?

slides.title: Dictionaries remember insertion order
slides.say: Since Python 3.7 the order of adding is a promise. Example: a guest who signs the book twice appears at the end. The older book idea of no first item is out of date for current Python. Ask the class: why do programs get simpler when the order is fixed?

slides.title: Dictionaries remember insertion order
slides.say: Add pear, apple and fig and print the keys in that order. Equality still ignores order. After del and adding pear again, it moves to the end. Ask the class to predict the last list before the run, then check where pear ended up.

slides.title: Story: one short reply gave dictionaries an order
slides.say: On 15 December 2017 Guido van Rossum answered a question about ordered dictionaries with the words Make it so. From Python 3.7 the order of adding is part of the language. Show the mailing-list page. Ask the class: why is a promise better than a lucky implementation detail?

slides.title: Hashable keys
slides.say: A key must be hashable, which means its value never changes. Example: a tuple of two numbers is fine, a list is refused. Equal numbers share one key. Ask the class: why would a changing key make a pair impossible to find?

slides.title: Keys must be hashable
slides.say: The tuple key works, the list key raises a TypeError, and the last dictionary has only one key because 1, 1.0 and True are equal. Ask the class: how many pairs do you expect in that last dictionary, and which value survives?

slides.title: Part 2: Reading and changing pairs
slides.say: Part two covers the everyday operations. We read keys, values and items, test for a key safely, set defaults, and add, remove and merge pairs. Ask the class: when is a missing key normal, and when is it a bug?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: reading the parts
slides.say: keys, values and items are three ways of reading the same shelf: the labels, the goods, or both together. A view is a window, list() a photograph. Example: the labels along a shelf edge. Ask the class: which of the three would you use in a loop, and why?

slides.title: Keys, values and items
slides.say: keys, values and items are three ways to read the same dictionary. Example: items gives the key and the value together, which is what most loops need. Ask the class: which of the three would you use to print a report line for each pair?

slides.title: Reading keys, values and items
slides.say: Run the code. keys and values print as lists, the loop prints one line per pair, and the last list shows each pair as a tuple with the key first. Ask the class: why do we wrap the views in list before printing?

slides.title: Does the key exist?
slides.say: Three ways to ask about a key: in, get and brackets. Example: picnic.get of eggs returns zero instead of an error. Choose the quiet tools for data where a key may be absent. Ask the class: when would a loud KeyError actually help you?

slides.title: Checking whether a key exists
slides.say: Read the table of printed answers. in and not in answer True or False, get returns the value or the fallback, and brackets on a missing key raise a KeyError that names the key. Ask the class which line they expected to fail.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: asking and changing
slides.say: Asking for a key is like asking the desk whether a ticket was issued. get() answers none politely, while brackets shout with a KeyError. Example: setdefault hangs a coat only on a free hook. Ask the class: which would you choose for a counting program?

slides.title: Setting a default value
slides.say: setdefault adds a pair only when the key is missing and always returns the stored value. Example: eggs gets 12 the first time and keeps it the second time, whatever default we offer later. Ask the class: which two jobs does one call do here, and why does that shorten counting loops?

slides.title: Setting default values with setdefault
slides.say: The first call stores 12 for eggs. The second call finds eggs and ignores 99. The chart shows the final picnic. Ask the class to predict what the second call prints before the run, then compare with the table. Example: eggs stays at twelve.

slides.title: Adding, removing and merging pairs
slides.say: Assignment adds or replaces, del and pop remove, and the pipe operator merges into a new dictionary. Example: spam pipe a second dictionary leaves spam unchanged and gives a new one. Ask the class: when would you prefer pop to del, and what does pop give back that del does not?

slides.title: Adding, removing and merging pairs
slides.say: Run the code and follow the table. pop returns the value it removed, the pipe operator builds a new dictionary where the right side wins, and spam itself is unchanged afterwards. Ask the class: which of these lines changes spam, and which does not?

slides.title: Views follow the dictionary
slides.say: A view is a live window and list is a photograph. Example: after adding fig, the view shows it and the photograph does not. sorted makes a new sorted list. Ask the class: when would you want the photograph instead of the window?

slides.title: Views follow the dictionary
slides.say: The view prints with fig, the frozen list without it. sorted gives a new alphabetical list, and reversed walks the newest key first. Ask the class to predict the first two lines before the run, then read the table together.

slides.title: Part 3: Programs that count and learn
slides.say: Part three uses the dictionary as a program's memory. birthdays.py learns new pairs, characterCount.py counts characters, and Counter and defaultdict shorten counting and grouping. Ask the class: what would you count first in your own life?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: programs that remember
slides.say: birthdays.py is a pocket diary that learns a friend's date the first time you ask. characterCount.py is tally marks on paper. Example: one stroke per sighting, one row per character. Ask the class: which everyday habit of yours is really a dictionary, and what are its keys?

slides.title: birthdays.py: a program that learns
slides.say: birthdays.py is a program that learns. A known name prints its date, an unknown name is stored with the next typed line. Example: Eve is learned and then found. Ask the class: what would happen to the program without the empty-name exit?

slides.title: birthdays.py with the typing scripted
slides.say: The typing a person would do is scripted in a list, so the run is repeatable. Follow the table: Alice is found, Eve is learned, then found again. Ask the class: where does the dictionary grow, and which line makes it grow?

slides.title: characterCount.py: counting by key
slides.say: Counting by key turns any text into a table of totals. Example: setdefault starts a new character at zero and then one is added. by_count tells sorted to put the biggest counts first. Ask the class: which character do you expect to lead in this sentence?

slides.title: characterCount.py counts every character
slides.say: Run the code and read the chart of the eight most common characters. The space leads with thirteen. The last line gives the length of the text and the number of different characters. Ask the class: why does a sentence have so few kinds?

slides.title: Story: the sentence the character counter counts
slides.say: The text in the character counter is the first sentence of Nineteen Eighty-Four, published in London on 8 June 1949. A real sentence makes the counts meaningful: thirteen spaces, and the same table would count the whole book. Ask the class: which letter do you expect to lead in your own name?

slides.title: Counter: counting in one call
slides.say: Counter is a dictionary built for counting. Example: Counter of abracadabra counts the letter a five times. It does in one call what the setdefault loop of the last slide did. Ask the class: which of your own lists would you count with it first?

slides.title: Counter does the counting
slides.say: Run the code and read the table beside the chart. most_common lists the leaders, a missing key counts as zero without being added, and the counts add up to the text length of eleven. Ask the class: what would c of z do on an ordinary dictionary?

slides.title: Grouping items under a key
slides.say: Grouping is counting with lists instead of numbers. Example: ant and ape both go under the key a. setdefault creates the list once and defaultdict creates it by itself. Ask the class: which of the two would you teach a friend first, and why?

slides.title: Grouping with setdefault and defaultdict
slides.say: Both loops build the same dictionary of lists, and the last line proves it by printing True. Compare how many lines each version needs and what each one creates for you. Ask the class: where does defaultdict create the empty list that setdefault created explicitly?

slides.title: Part 4: Structuring data
slides.say: Part four is about structuring data. We model a chessboard, validate it, nest dictionaries for a picnic, and turn lists of loot into inventories. Ask the class: which real thing would you model with a dictionary?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: models and structures
slides.say: A data model is the floor plan drawn before building: it decides which details exist at all. A street map keeps the streets and drops the parked cars. Example: nested dictionaries are Russian dolls. Ask the class: what would you leave out of a model of a classroom?

slides.title: Modelling a chessboard
slides.say: A data model keeps what matters and drops the rest. Example: only occupied squares are keys, so an empty square is simply absent. The picture is Figure 7-2 of the book. Ask the class: what would a model of a library keep, and what would it drop?

slides.title: Modelling a chessboard
slides.say: Run the code. c6 is in the board, a1 is empty by the get fallback, and sorted shows the five keys. The book figure shows the same position. Ask the class: why is the board model small, and why is that good?

slides.title: Story: where the squares a1 to h8 come from
slides.say: Philipp Stamma used the modern square names in the 1730s, Howard Staunton described the system in 1847, and FIDE stopped recognising descriptive notation in 1981. The chessboard dictionary borrows those names as keys. Ask the class: which notation do you already use that could serve as a key?

slides.title: One dictionary, many pictures
slides.say: The dictionary is the data and the printout is one view. Example: a seating chart printed from a guest list. Looking up each square with a fallback fills the empty squares. Ask the class: how would you draw the same data as a picture instead of text?

slides.title: Printing the board from the dictionary
slides.say: Run the code and read the table drawn as a board. Each rank is eight lookups and an empty square prints as two dots. The dictionary never changes. Ask the class: where on the board are the three pieces, and which key stores each?

slides.title: Commands are dictionary operations
slides.say: Moving a piece is a copy followed by a delete. Example: e2 becomes e4. We play on a copy so the starting position stays safe. Ask the class: what would happen to START if we had written board equals START without copy?

slides.title: Chess commands are dictionary operations
slides.say: Follow the three boxes. START is copied, the pawn moves from e2 to e4, and format builds the report. The last two lines show that the board changed and START did not. Ask the class why copy.copy is enough here.

slides.title: A validator checks the rules
slides.say: A validator turns each rule of the game into a test on keys or values. Example: z9 is not a real square, and a legal position has one king of each colour. Ask the class: which other rule of chess could you check with a dictionary?

slides.title: A chess dictionary validator
slides.say: Run the code and read the table of rules. The bad square z9 is found among the keys, and the kings are collected from the values. Ask the class: which rule looks at the keys and which looks at the values?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the practice projects
slides.say: The practice projects are small workshops. The chessboard is a pocket chess set, the validator an arbiter, the inventory a backpack list and the loot conversion a sorting of heaps into labelled bins. Ask the class: which one would you build first, and why?

slides.title: Nested dictionaries
slides.say: Nested dictionaries hold a record inside a record. Example: guests of Alice reaches her basket, and a second key reaches pretzels. get with zero avoids a KeyError for guests who did not bring an item. Ask the class: how deep could such a nesting go?

slides.title: Nested dictionaries: the picnic
slides.say: Run the code and read the chart of the baskets. The total of apples is seven and nobody brought cups, so that total is zero. Alice brought twelve pretzels. Ask the class: what would total do without the get fallback?

slides.title: Fantasy game inventory
slides.say: The inventory maps items to counts. Example: a rope, six torches and forty-two gold coins. The total is the sum of the counts, not the number of keys. Example: three keys but forty-nine items. Ask the class: what would the total be if we counted keys instead of values, and which mistake is that?

slides.title: Fantasy game inventory
slides.say: Run the code and read the bar chart. Each line prints the count and the item, and the last line prints the total of forty-nine. Example: the rope counts one, the torches six. Ask the class: which line of the loop adds the count to the total?

slides.title: From a list to counts
slides.say: A list of loot is added into the inventory. Example: get of item with zero as default reads the count of the new ruby as zero, so it starts at one. Known items grow. Ask the class: why does the same pair of lines turn any list into counts, whatever the list holds?

slides.title: List-to-dictionary loot conversion
slides.say: Run the code and compare the chart of before and after. Gold coin grew to forty-four and two new items joined, forty-seven items in all. Ask the class to predict the total before the run, then check it against the printed number.

slides.title: Part 5: Copies and writing data down
slides.say: Part five finishes the chapter. We copy dictionaries with care, write them as JSON, name their keys with TypedDict, and match their shape with the match statement. Ask the class: what goes wrong when two names share one dictionary?

slides.title: Everyday pictures: closing the chapter
slides.say: A summary is the last line of a recipe card: what you must remember. Practice questions are mock driving questions, and practice programs are a workshop evening. Example: the five practice questions on a later slide. Ask the class: what is your own last line for this chapter?

slides.title: Alias, shallow copy and deep copy
slides.say: An alias is a second name for one dictionary. A shallow copy has a new outside but shares the inside. Only deepcopy is fully independent. Example: change the apples inside the original. Ask the class: who sees the change, and who does not?

slides.title: Alias, shallow copy and deep copy
slides.say: Run the code and read the table. The alias and the shallow copy see ninety-nine apples, the deep copy still sees five. The last lines show that the shallow copy shares the inner dictionary. Ask the class to predict the three numbers first.

slides.title: Writing data down with JSON
slides.say: JSON is plain text made of pairs and lists, the same pieces as a dictionary. Example: dumps writes the cat as text, loads builds an equal dictionary back. pprint is for people reading nested data. Ask the class: why is plain text a good carrier between programs?

slides.title: Writing data down with json and pprint
slides.say: Run the code. The first line is the JSON text, the second says the rebuilt dictionary equals the original, and pprint prints the nested data one key to a line. Ask the class: which quotes does JSON use, and why does that matter?

slides.title: Story: the notation that carries dictionaries
slides.say: Douglas Crockford and Chip Morningstar sent the first JSON message in April 2001. Yahoo began offering web services in JSON in December 2005, and the IETF published RFC 8259 in December 2017. Show json.dumps on a dictionary. Ask the class: why is plain text a good carrier?

slides.title: Typed records and read-only views
slides.say: A TypedDict names the keys of a record, but Python does not enforce it while running. Example: Cat has a name and an age. A mapping proxy is a read-only window. Ask the class: which mistake would a type checker catch before the program runs?

slides.title: Typed records and read-only views
slides.say: Run the code and read the table. At run time the cat is an ordinary dict, and the proxy shows the same age and length but cannot be changed. Ask the class: who enforces the keys of a TypedDict, and who enforces the proxy?

slides.title: Matching the shape of a dictionary
slides.say: A mapping pattern tests which keys a dictionary has and binds their values. Example: the first case needs name and age with an age above five. The first case that fits wins. Ask the class: what would print if the age were four?

slides.title: Matching the shape of a dictionary
slides.say: Run the code. The cat has both keys and an age above five, so case one fits and case two is never tried. Extra keys would be allowed. Ask the class: how would you change the guard so that Zophie is no senior cat?

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: The book's outputs still hold, but six things moved on: the order promise, reversible views, the merge operators, the match statement, TypedDict and the hashing rule. Example: the pipe operator merges two dictionaries into a new one. Ask the class: which of these will you use first?

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Here are the five lines that answer the five questions of the start. Example: copy.copy shares the inner dictionaries, deepcopy does not. If one line feels unproven, go back to the slide that carries its example. Ask the class: which line would you test first?

slides.title: Practice questions
slides.say: The book ends with questions and programs. Answer the questions from the examples you have seen, then write the three programs yourself: the validator, the inventory and the loot conversion. Example: spam['foo'] on a dictionary without foo. Ask the class: what do you predict it prints?

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: These links lead to the textbook, the official documentation, the history behind the stories, a talk on modern dictionaries and a tool to step through your code. The last one is this course's own repository. Pick one link and read it before next class. Ask: which will you open first?
